analysis.one_liner: Requires pathogen reduction treatment and certification for processed foods, meat, and poultry.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate, and not a single senator cosponsored it before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required food processors to treat every food they make, process, or hold to reduce pathogens like Salmonella and E. coli, and to certify to the government that the food contains no verifiable traces of pathogens. Meat and poultry sellers would have to certify that each ingredient was treated or tested clean. It would also have ended the practice of labeling ingredients vaguely as 'spices, flavorings, and coloring,' requiring each one to be named on the package. The rules would have taken effect 18 months after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would face lower risk of foodborne illness from contaminated processed food, meat, and poultry, plus clearer ingredient labels.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires pathogen reduction treatments on each ingredient of processed foods sold in the United States, with the HHS Secretary writing the specific rules [S2][S3].
Anyone selling or transporting meat, poultry, or their products would have to certify that each ingredient was pathogen-treated or tested free of verifiable pathogen traces [S2][S3].
The bill ends the practice of grouping ingredients under the generic labels 'spices, flavorings, and coloring' for meat, poultry, and other foods, requiring each to be named [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat, poultry, and processed food companies, which would bear the cost of pathogen testing and treatment, likely passing some of it to consumers in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Requiring treatment or a no-traces certification for every ingredient of every processed food is an extremely strict standard that would impose significant testing and treatment costs on processors and retailers [S3].
The rules take effect 18 months after enactment, giving the industry limited time to build testing and treatment capacity, and the compliance burden would fall hardest on smaller processors [S3].
Industry compliance costs would likely be passed through to consumers as somewhat higher prices for meat and packaged foods [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Reducing foodborne illness is a real public benefit, and clearer ingredient labels help people with allergies and dietary restrictions. But the bill's certification standard is drawn very strictly, and honest supporters would acknowledge the compliance costs would be substantial and partly passed to shoppers. A more workable version could have achieved much of the safety gain at lower cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill in the Senate on November 30, 2009 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral, and Congress ended on January 3, 2011, with the bill never reported out of committee or voted on [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat, poultry, and processed food companies, which avoided new pathogen testing, treatment, and certification requirements, and the continuation of vague 'spices and flavorings' labeling.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was her lone bill on this subject with no cosponsors.

against.name: Blanche Lincoln
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill, leaving it dead in committee.

against.name: Meat and processed food industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory pathogen-treatment and testing mandates as costly and technically impractical for every ingredient.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and no other senator signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would require pathogen treatment or clean-testing certification for every meat and poultry ingredient sold, a costly new compliance obligation. The industry's interest in avoiding those costs runs against the public's interest in safer meat [S2][S3].

Registered food facilities would have to apply pathogen reduction treatments and certify their products, adding testing and treatment costs across the packaged food supply. Their gain in avoiding the mandate is the public's loss of a safety guarantee [S2][S3].
Retail stores are included in the certification requirement, adding some burden, but clearer ingredient labeling helps retailers' customers make informed choices [S3].
Mandatory pathogen testing and treatment across the food supply would have created demand for laboratories and treatment technologies, a cost that reflects a safety benefit to consumers [S3].
